passage:
Gopika had applied to thirty-one jobs since graduating and heard back from none. So when the message came while she stood in the ration shop queue, she read it three times.
"Congratulations! Selected for work-from-home data entry. Rs 38,000 per month, 2 hours daily. Pay Rs 1,999 registration to confirm your seat. Offer valid 1 hour."
She thought of Appa's cough, the loan on the tractor, her younger brother Tejas's school fees. Two hours a day. She could do that between chores.
She paid from the money kept for her exam forms.
The next message asked for her bank login "to set up salary". Then a security deposit of Rs 5,000. Gopika sat on the temple steps, the phone warm in her hand, and felt her stomach turn. The hurry, the fees, a salary that needed her password.
She didn't send more. But she couldn't make herself tell Amma about the 1,999, not yet.

qa.q: How much registration fee did the message ask for?
qa.a: It asked for Rs 1,999 registration to confirm her seat.

qa.q: Why was Gopika tempted by the offer?
qa.a: She felt desperate after thirty-one unanswered applications and worried about Appa's cough, the tractor loan and Tejas's fees, so easy pay looked like a lifeline.

qa.q: What protective steps could Gopika take now?
qa.a: She should share no bank details, report the message to the cybercrime helpline and her bank, and tell Amma so she is not carrying it alone.

qa.q: What would change if the message had said no fees and an interview at an office?
qa.a: It would look more like a real employer, since real jobs don't charge to hire or ask for passwords, and Gopika could check it calmly.

grounding: A young graduate desperate for work in a small town pays a registration fee for an easy high-paying job, then sees the warning signs when her bank login and more money are asked.

passage:
Siddiq's rent was due Friday, and between lectures the café had cut his shifts to one a week. So the email felt like luck: "Remote Payments Assistant. 600 pounds a week. No experience. Receive client payments into your account and forward them, keeping 10 percent."
He read it on the night bus through the Manchester drizzle. It was easy. Almost too easy. They wanted his bank details and a photo of his passport today, "for payroll".
At the flat, his flatmate Mina was making toast. "You look happy."
"Job offer. Great pay." He showed her.
Mina read it twice. "Siddiq, they want to move their money through your account?"
"It's their clients' money."
"Then why can't they use their own bank?"
He opened his mouth and found no answer. The rent was still due Friday. He wanted, badly, for this to be real.

qa.q: What did the company want from Siddiq today?
qa.a: They wanted his bank details and a photo of his passport, "for payroll".

qa.q: How did Siddiq feel about the offer, and why did he want it to be real so badly?
qa.a: Siddiq felt hopeful and desperate at once; his rent was due Friday and his café shifts had been cut, so the easy money felt like rescue.

qa.q: What should Siddiq do after Mina's question?
qa.a: He should not share his bank details or passport, let no one move money through his account, and report the email and ask the university's student support for help with rent.

qa.q: How does Mina see the offer?
qa.a: Mina sees it as suspicious, because no real company needs to route money through a student's personal account.

grounding: A student short of rent gets a high-paying easy job that wants his bank details and passport, and his hope makes the warning signs easy to miss.

passage:
"Lalit, look at this! Data entry, work from home, two hours a day, ₹35,000 a month!" Devika held out her phone.
"Who's the company?"
"Some international firm. The recruiter messaged me on the job site. I just have to pay ₹2,500 registration and send my bank details for salary."
"You have to pay them?"
"It's a small fee. Lalit, I've applied to sixty jobs since June. Sixty. Nobody's called back. This is the first yes." Her voice cracked.
Lalit sat down beside her. "I know how tired you are. But real companies pay you. They don't charge you to hire you."
"Maybe this one's different."
"Let's check it. Company registration, their official website, a phone call to their office, not the recruiter's number."
Devika was quiet. Then she nodded slowly. "If it's fake, I don't know what I'll do."
"Then we keep looking. Together."

qa.q: How much registration fee did the recruiter ask for?
qa.a: ₹2,500 registration.

qa.q: Why was Devika so ready to believe the offer?
qa.a: Devika felt desperate and exhausted after sixty applications with no replies, so the first yes felt like relief.

qa.q: What did Lalit suggest before paying anything?
qa.a: Checking the company's registration, its official website, and calling its office directly, not the recruiter's number.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the offer?
qa.a: Lalit sees the upfront fee and request for bank details as warning signs, since real companies don't charge to hire.

grounding: It shows a young adult, desperate after many rejections, offered easy high pay if she pays a registration fee and shares bank details.

passage:
I'm Kunal, and I lost ₹3,000 I didn't have, in my final year.
I'd been job-hunting for months. My father had retired, and I felt I needed to earn fast. Then a message came on a messaging app: "Part-time online work. ₹1,500 a day. Only one hour. Registration: ₹3,000, fully refundable."
It sounded too good. But I was so desperate that I wanted it to be true. The woman on the phone was polite and professional. She sent an official-looking offer letter with a logo.
I paid. Then they asked for a "security deposit" and my bank login "for salary setup." That's when my stomach dropped.
I called my friend Nirmala, whose brother works in a bank. She said, "Don't send anything more. Block them. Call your bank now." We reported it on the cyber crime portal that night.
I felt stupid for weeks. Now I tell everyone: if they charge you to hire you, it isn't a job.

qa.q: What did the recruiters ask for after the registration fee?
qa.a: A "security deposit" and a bank login "for salary setup."

qa.q: Why did Kunal pay the registration fee?
qa.a: Kunal felt desperate to earn after Kunal's father retired, and wanted the offer to be true even though it seemed too good.

qa.q: What did Nirmala advise, and what did Kunal do?
qa.a: Nirmala advised sending nothing more, blocking them and calling the bank, and they reported it on the cyber crime portal that night.

qa.q: How might Kunal's father feel if he heard the story?
qa.a: Kunal's father might feel worried and sad about that pressure, but relieved that he stopped and reported it.

grounding: A young adult recalls losing a registration fee to a fake high-pay job offer out of desperation, before being asked for bank details.

passage:
Placement officer's note, Wednesday. Written by Manjula.
Kamal, B.Com final year, came to my office in a hurry this morning. He had an offer from a "multinational" for a remote accounts assistant role: ₹50,000 a month, flexible hours. They asked him to pay a ₹5,000 refundable training deposit today and to share his bank account and PAN details so they could "set up salary."
He said, "Ma'am, my family really needs this. Please say it's real."
I could see how badly he wanted it. I explained, gently, that real employers do not charge fees to hire, and that sharing bank details this way can lead to his account being misused.
We searched for the company on the official registry together. It wasn't registered. Their "office address" was a residential flat.
He sat with his head in his hands. I told him he had done the right thing by coming. We reported the offer on the cyber crime portal and I've added him to our verified campus drive next week.

qa.q: How much training deposit did the company ask Kamal to pay?
qa.a: A ₹5,000 refundable training deposit.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when he came to the placement office?
qa.a: Kamal felt desperate and hopeful, pleading for the offer to be real because his family really needs the money.

qa.q: What steps did the placement officer take with Kamal?
qa.a: Explaining that real employers don't charge fees, checking the official registry together, reporting the offer, and adding him to a verified campus drive.

qa.q: How might Kamal's family feel if he had paid?
qa.a: His family might have lost money they needed and felt even more pressure, so stopping protected them too.

grounding: A placement officer notes a student offered high pay for easy work who was asked to pay a deposit and share bank details, with desperation making it believable.

passage:
Friday
Sixty-two applications since March, and today someone finally wants me. "Data entry, work from home, two hours a day," the message said, with a salary bigger than Papa's. All I have to do is pay a registration fee by tonight and send my bank details "for salary setup".
I actually cried a bit. Relief, I think. I'm so tired of Mummy's face when relatives ask what I'm doing now.
Yash-bhaiya came in and I showed him. He didn't say it was fake straight away. He asked, "Which company? Did you apply to them?" I didn't. I'd never heard of them. The email is from some random free account. Two hours a day for that money... I wanted it to be true so badly I didn't let myself ask.
We looked up the company name together. Nothing. I'm not paying anything and not sending bank details. Tomorrow Yash-bhaiya and I will report the number, screenshots and all.
Payal

qa.q: How many applications had Payal sent since March?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: Why did Payal almost believe the offer?
qa.a: Payal felt desperate and exhausted after so many applications, and the offer brought such relief that the questions got pushed aside.

qa.q: What checks helped, and what did Payal decide?
qa.a: Asking which company it was and whether Payal had applied, then searching the name, showed nothing real; Payal decided not to pay or share bank details and to report it.

qa.q: How did Yash-bhaiya help without making things worse?
qa.a: He didn't mock the offer; he asked simple questions and searched with Payal, so the discovery felt shared rather than shaming.

grounding: Shows a job seeker offered high pay for little work who is asked for a fee and bank details, with desperation making it easy to believe.
